_readme: How a character's outfit text becomes the garments of a designed body (npcgen/outfit.py). The Body Designer makes a sleeveless shirt, fitted trousers, an open jacket, a bib apron, a knee-length skirt and a sleeveless knee-length dress, so this table says which words of a sheet name a shirt, which name trousers, which name a jacket, an apron, a skirt or a dress (`makes`), and which name something it cannot make yet (said, never guessed). `top`: a shirt-like word. `cover`: a sleeveless layer that covers the chest (a vest, a bodice): its colour is the chest's. `outer`: a jacket or a coat, which shows the shirt: a stand-in for one only when none is named. `wrap`: a cloak or an apron, never a stand-in. `makes`: which of those words are put on as the Body Designer's open jacket (a short jacket open at the front: jacket, blazer, cardigan) and its bib apron (apron), as its knee-length skirt (skirt: a kilt, shorts, a sarong and a loincloth are not skirts, so they are said and not made) and as its sleeveless dress (dress and gown: a robe, a toga, a kimono, a cassock, a swimsuit, a bikini and a leotard are not that dress, so they are said and not made); a coat is longer and is not made, and a word of `makes` stands in for the colour of the shirt only when it is not put on (put on, the jacket goes over a shirt that keeps its own colour). A word of `makes` in a part of the text that also names a dress ('a blazer dress') belongs to the dress and is not put on. A skirt takes the place of trousers (a sheet that names both gets the skirt, and says so) and is worn with a shirt; a dress takes the place of the shirt and the trousers, and is worn on its own. The skirt of a gown is the gown's own. `armour`: worn over everything, not made. `bottom`: trousers. `whole`: one garment for the chest and the legs (a uniform: a shirt and trousers in its colour). `dress`: covers the chest and the legs, so no stand-in is put on; `skirt`: covers the legs only. `ignore` are phrases that only look like garments ('top hat'). `rename` are phrases with a dress word in them that name something else ('dress shoes', 'a dress shirt', 'a dress uniform', 'a surgical gown'): they are read as what they are (`shoes`, `shirt`, `uniform`, `robe`), so that dress shoes are never taken for a dress. A word also names its plural. A garment's colour is read from its own part of the text (the parts are split at a comma, 'and', 'over', 'with'...): the colour words and modifiers of `cloth`, the explicit ones before the colour of a material the part names (`materials`: 'canvas' is tan, 'jeans' denim), in the order cover, top, outer, whole; when it names none, the Body Designer's plain colour is used.
